Whitehead (Etrumeus whiteheadi) exhibits the typical pelagic spawning strategy of clupeids, with fertilised ova developing as planktonic eggs. Field surveys examining early life stages have documented that newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, immediately following eclosion, possess a notably low body mass. The wet weight at birth, measured from transparent, yolk-laden eggs that average 1.4 millimetres in diameter, has been estimated at approximately 0.0014 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0014 grams]. This minimal starting mass is consistent with values reported for the Round herring (Etrumeus teres), reflecting the relatively small investment per offspring characteristic of small-bodied clupeids that produce large numbers of pelagic eggs. Laboratory incubation experiments conducted at a stable temperature of 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C] have demonstrated that the age at birth, defined as the duration between fertilisation and chorion rupture, is 30 days [ab = 30 days]. This protracted incubation period, comparable to that of other temperate clupeids under similar thermal regimes, allows for considerable yolk absorption prior to the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical period when endotrophic larvae are particularly vulnerable to predation and starvation.

Comprehensive field sampling across the species' range, from the Benguela Current region to the southern coast of South Africa, indicates that the largest individuals attain a standard length of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters]. This asymptotic dimension, achieved by older spawning adults, places Whitehead within the typical size spectrum of small-to-medium pelagic forage fish. Comparatively, this ultimate length is substantially less than that of the closely related Pacific round herring (Etrumeus sadina), which may exceed 30 centimeters, but is larger than many sympatric anchovy species. The relationship between body size and reproductive investment is evident when considering that the ultimate wet weight, calculated from length-weight regressions of post-pubertal individuals, is approximately 100 grams [Wwi = approximately 100 grams]. This value, derived from a robust sample of mature fish captured during ichthyoplankton surveys, reflects the allometric accumulation of somatic tissue and gonadal reserves.

Sexual maturation in Whitehead involves a well-defined set of developmental milestones, with the standard length at puberty serving as a key indicator of the transition from the immature post-metamorphic stage to the reproductively viable adult. Based on histological examination of gonad tissue from juvenile fish collected during recruitment events, the standard length at which 50% of individuals exhibit the onset of gametogenesis onset is 14.5 centimeters [Lp = 14.5 centimeters]. This length threshold, occurring before the attainment of asymptotic size, ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to sustain the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and spermiation. By comparison, the standard length at puberty in Whitehead is considerably smaller than that of the congeneric Etrumeus micropus, a species found in the Indian Ocean, which shows a later maturation schedule. The shift from the actively growing larval phase and juvenile stage to a sexually mature fish involves not only morphological transformation but also a substantial reallocation of resources from somatic growth to reproductive effort, a pattern typical of iteroparous teleosts.

The complete lifespan of Whitehead, from the moment of syngamy to natural mortality, has been investigated through otolith micro-increment analysis, a technique that reveals the age structure of wild populations with high precision. Studies conducted in the productive waters of the Benguela upwelling system, where thermal conditions are relatively stable, estimate that the oldest documented individuals live for approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days] at 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to roughly five years, positions Whitehead as a short-lived species relative to many larger ichthyoplankton predators, but is typical among small clupeids that exhibit high natural mortality rates. The relationship between this maximum lifespan and the species' reproductive strategy is notable: the combination of a five-year lifespan with an early age at first reproduction suggests a life history that maximises cumulative reproductive output over a relatively compressed temporal window. In contrast, deeper-bodied clupeids such as Sardinops sagax may exceed ten years, highlighting the varied pace of life among sardine-like fishes.

From a comparative demographic perspective, the life-history parameters of Whitehead converge to define a species that is well adapted to productive, temperate marine ecosystems. The length-at-maturity and asymptotic mass data show that Whitehead is a moderately small clupeid, with a maximum standard length of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters] and an adult wet weight of 100 grams [Wwi = 100 grams], values that align with the typical dimensions of forage fish in the Benguela Current. The modest wet weight at birth of 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams] coupled with an extended incubation period of 30 days [ab = 30 days] at 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C] reflects a trade-off between offspring size and developmental stability. The standard length at puberty of 14.5 centimeters [Lp = 14.5 centimeters] ensures that reproduction begins well before the species reaches its maximum size, while an estimated maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] constrains the total number of breeding seasons at a temperature of 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C]. These collectively suggest that Whitehead follows a moderately paced life-history strategy, balancing relatively slow development for a clupeid with a short reproductive window, a combination that is particularly successful in the pulsed food environments of the southern African sardine run.
